did_you_know.text: The psalm opens with a call to sing a “new song”—a song renewed in response to the wonders and salvation the Lord has brought about. The expressions “his right hand” and “his holy arm” vividly portray the Lord’s active power.

The Lord’s salvation is not presented as something hidden: he makes it known, and his righteousness is revealed “in the sight of the nations.” In this way, the Lord’s work is described as a testimony visible even to the peoples.

Salvation is connected with two foundations: the Lord’s steadfast love and faithfulness to the house of Israel. At the same time, its scope is universal—“all the ends of the earth” see the salvation of our God.
The call to praise expands from the speakers to “all the earth.” The verbs “shout,” “burst into joyful song,” “sing,” and “make music” create a succession of joyful and enthusiastic sounds.
The psalm mentions the lyre as an instrument accompanying the singing: “make music to the Lord with the lyre.” The praise is not only verbal but is joined with instrumental music and singing.

Trumpets and the ram’s horn are also added, and the Lord is called “the King.” The combination of blasts, musical instruments, and the title “King” gives the praise a festive and ceremonial character.
The sea, the world, and its inhabitants join in the description of joy. Nature is portrayed vividly: the sea resounds, making it seem as though the whole world is taking part in the praise.
The rivers and mountains are given human qualities: the rivers seem to clap their hands, and the mountains sing for joy. This use of imagery and personification portrays worldwide rejoicing.

The psalm’s conclusion links the singing with the Lord’s judgment. The Lord comes to judge the world with righteousness and the peoples with fairness, so the joy is presented as a response to just rule, not merely as a celebration.
